clue.text: Where students learn hot music ?

parts.note: two pictures in one: a music school where students train, and a glass room built onto a house that stays hot for plants

explanation.surface: A question about where young jazz players go to study hot music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot music' suggests jazz, but the clue joins a school of music with a heated glass garden room, both called by the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: A school for musical training shares its name with a warm glass extension for growing plants.

clue.text: Delius heard the first of these

definitions.text: Delius heard the first of these

parts.words: Delius heard the first of these
parts.note: refers to the orchestral piece by Frederick Delius titled On Hearing the First ... in Spring, named for a spring bird call

explanation.surface: A remark about the composer Delius listening to the first of something.
explanation.walkthrough: Frederick Delius, an English composer, wrote 'On Hearing the First Cuckoo in Spring'; the clue quotes that title.
explanation.definitionFit: The bird whose call heralds spring gives its name to the Delius tone poem's title.

clue.text: Nicked by companion observed outside

indicators.note: observed is placed outside, so its letters surround the companion abbreviation

parts.note: something observed has been noted
CH is the abbreviation for Companion of Honour, a British order

explanation.surface: Someone was arrested by a companion who had been watching from outside.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicked here means cut with a small V-shaped mark, the same as notched.

clue.text: Clear former 'copper found with plate perhaps

parts.note: ex- is the prefix meaning former
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

indicators.note: perhaps marks plate as a possible arrangement of its letters rather than the word itself

explanation.surface: A retired policeman is found alongside some plate, maybe stolen silver.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' suggests a policeman; it is the metal, symbol CU. 'perhaps' rearranges PLATE to LPATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To exculpate someone is to free them from blame, which is to clear their name.

clue.text: Vessels for five to sail at sea ?

parts.note: V is the Roman numeral five

indicators.note: at sea means confused or all over the place, so the letters of sail are jumbled

explanation.surface: A question about which boats five people might sail in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vessels' and 'sail at sea' paint ships, but the vessels are small glass bottles; 'at sea' rearranges SAIL to IALS.
explanation.definitionFit: Small glass containers for liquids or medicine are called vials, a kind of vessel.

clue.text: Something shockingly fishy about this weapon

definitions.text: Something shockingly fishy about this weapon

parts.words: Something shockingly fishy about this weapon
parts.note: the underwater missile shares its name with the electric ray, a fish that gives shocks

explanation.surface: A suspicion that a weapon is not quite what it seems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fishy' reads as suspicious; here it is literal, since the electric ray, a fish that delivers shocks, is also called a torpedo.
explanation.definitionFit: The self-propelled underwater missile was named after the electric ray, which stuns prey with a shock.

clue.text: His girl in Algiers was Italian

definitions.text: His girl in Algiers was Italian

parts.words: His girl in Algiers was Italian
parts.note: points to the comic opera L'italiana in Algeri, The Italian Girl in Algiers, and its composer

explanation.surface: A man's girlfriend living in Algeria turns out to be from Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'L'italiana in Algeri' (The Italian Girl in Algiers) is an 1813 comic opera by Gioachino Rossini.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian composer wrote the opera whose title character is the Italian girl in Algiers.

clue.text: Supporters follow to provide food for these creeps

indicators.note: follow means the supporters come after the catering word in the answer

parts.note: to cater is to provide food
pillars are columns that hold up a structure

explanation.surface: Fans arrive afterwards to lay on food for some unpleasant people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Creeps' suggests unpleasant people; the creatures creep along, as larvae do.
explanation.definitionFit: Butterfly and moth larvae crawl slowly along stems, so they are creatures that creep.

clue.text: Hermit has a little science to quote in return

parts.note: Sc is a short form of science, as in BSc

indicators.note: in return means the quoting word is written backwards

parts.note: to quote a source is to cite it

explanation.surface: A recluse knows only a bit of science and repeats it back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in return' turns CITE into ETIC, after A and SC.
explanation.definitionFit: A hermit lives in severe self-denial, the life of an ascetic.

clue.text: Seizes what Bobby makes

definitions.meaning: seizes means takes hold of or captures
a bobby is a British police officer, who takes suspects into custody

explanation.walkthrough: A 'bobby' is everyday British slang for a police officer, after Sir Robert Peel.
explanation.definitionFit: To seize someone is to take them into custody, which is exactly what a police officer does on the beat.

clue.text: Unusually stately, I lack a stately capital

definitions.note: a capital city of one of the United States, with a play on stately

indicators.note: unusually signals that the following letters appear in an unusual order

explanation.surface: Someone admits to lacking a grand capital, in an unusually stately way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unusually' rearranges STATELY I LACK. 'stately capital' plays on the word: it is the capital of a state, Utah.
explanation.definitionFit: Utah's seat of government is a city whose capital status belongs to a US state.

clue.text: Ruined chapel contains nothing of such colossal importance

indicators.note: contains means the jumbled chapel letters hold another letter inside
ruined means wrecked, so the chapel's letters are knocked into a new order

parts.note: O is zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A ruined chapel that houses nothing of great historical weight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruined' rearranges CHAPEL to EPCHAL, and 'contains' puts O inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something epochal marks a new era, so it is of momentous significance.

clue.text: Particular pals dispersed around Clerkenwell area

indicators.note: around means the scattered letters go round the district code
dispersed means scattered, so the letters of pals are spread into a new order

parts.note: Clerkenwell is in London's EC1 postal district, with the 1 read as I

explanation.surface: Close friends spread out around a district of central London.
explanation.walkthrough: Clerkenwell is a district of London whose postcode is EC1; '1' becomes I. 'dispersed' turns PALS into SPAL, which goes 'around' ECI.
explanation.definitionFit: Particular in the sense of specific or distinct means special, singled out from the rest.

clue.text: Sat, but assumed not to eat

indicators.note: not means the eating word is left out of the longer word

parts.note: assumed means supposed
to sup is to eat supper

explanation.surface: Someone sat down but was presumed not to be dining.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' removes SUP (to eat) from SUPPOSED (assumed). 'Sat' is the definition: to sit for a portrait.
explanation.definitionFit: A model who sat for an artist held a pose for them.

clue.text: Such food is divine

parts.note: the food of the Greek gods was ambrosia, so food fit for gods is described with its adjective

explanation.surface: Praise for a delicious meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Divine' reads as delicious; it also means of the gods, whose food in Greek myth was ambrosia.
explanation.definitionFit: Ambrosia was the food of the Olympian gods, so ambrosial food is heavenly.

clue.text: Battle helmet

definitions.meaning: a battle of the Crimean War fought in 1854
a knitted head covering exposing only the face

explanation.walkthrough: The knitted helmet takes its name from the Crimean War battle, where troops wore them in the cold.
explanation.definitionFit: Balaclava is both the Crimean War battle site and the woollen headgear named after it, worn by soldiers there.

clue.text: Touches down skilfully on roll of water offshore ?

parts.note: an aircraft that touches down lands
well means skilfully

explanation.surface: A pilot sets down neatly on a rolling sea near the coast.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a seaplane landing; the definition is a rise of the sea near the shore.
explanation.definitionFit: A swell is a long rolling wave, and one felt near the coast is a ground swell rolling in.

clue.text: Blue' artist

definitions.meaning: a soft light blue shade named after a French portrait painter

explanation.definitionFit: Jean-Marc Nattier, the French painter, gave his name to the pale blue shade he favoured.

clue.text: Tim, at cricket practice, rises and is struck

indicators.note: in a down entry rises means the letters read upwards, backwards
Tim at practice is in the nets, so the name goes inside

parts.note: nets are the netted enclosures where cricketers practise

explanation.surface: Tim, practising at cricket, gets up and is hit by the ball.
explanation.walkthrough: Cricket 'nets' are practice enclosures. TIM goes inside NETS giving NETTIMS; 'rises' turns that upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Smitten is the old past participle of smite, so it means struck or hit.

clue.text: Descriptive of cheque drawn unproductively ?

parts.note: a cheque signed with no amount filled in, and the idiom for searching with no result, drawing nothing

explanation.surface: A question about a cheque written out to no purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: A cheque 'drawn' is written out; to 'draw' a ___ is also to get no result from a search.
explanation.definitionFit: An unfilled cheque has its amount left empty, and fruitless efforts are said to come up empty.

clue.text: Scottish writer has right to a fence

parts.note: J M Barrie, the Scottish author of Peter Pan

explanation.surface: A Scottish author has a legal right to put up a fence.
explanation.definitionFit: A fence is an obstruction keeping things out, a kind of barricade.

clue.text: No object in bothering Melissa

indicators.note: bothering means upsetting, so the letters of Melissa are disturbed

explanation.surface: There is no point in pestering a woman named Melissa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bothering' rearranges MELISSA.
explanation.definitionFit: Having no object means having no purpose or goal, which is to be purposeless.

clue.text: Busybodies are at home here

parts.note: busybodies read as busy bodies, the industrious insects, and their mound nest

explanation.surface: Nosy neighbours feel comfortable in this place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Busybodies' suggests meddlers; read as busy bodies it means hard-working insects, famously industrious.
explanation.definitionFit: Industrious little insects live together in a mound nest of earth.

clue.text: A movement in popular golf clubs

indicators.note: in signals that the answer sits inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A trend catching on among well-liked golf clubs.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across 'popuLAR GOlf'. 'Movement' is a section of a musical work.
explanation.definitionFit: A slow section of a symphony or sonata is marked with this Italian tempo term.

clue.text: Relating to Beatrix's art ?

parts.note: Beatrix Potter's surname read as the trade of a maker of clay pots

explanation.surface: A question about the illustrations of a children's author.
explanation.walkthrough: Beatrix Potter wrote and illustrated Peter Rabbit; the clue reads her surname as a pot-maker, whose craft is pottery.
explanation.definitionFit: Pottery is the craft of firing clay, and the adjective for clayware is this word.

clue.text: Maybe ref's wit is comparatively quick

indicators.note: maybe suggests one possible arrangement of the letters of ref's wit

explanation.surface: Perhaps the referee's humour is quicker than most.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' rearranges REFSWIT; the possessive apostrophe adds no letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The comparative form of fast or speedy, more rapid.

clue.text: 21's inmate takes in fruit for nourishment

indicators.note: takes in means the insect word holds the fruit inside it

parts.note: the inmate of an anthill (21 across) is an ant
a lime is a citrus fruit

explanation.surface: A prisoner of the anthill swallows some fruit to stay fed.
explanation.walkthrough: '21's inmate' points to 21 across, the anthill, whose inhabitant is an ANT.
explanation.definitionFit: Aliment is an old word for food or sustenance.

clue.text: He madly burns our oats, the monster

indicators.note: madly means wildly, so the letters of burns our oats are thrown about

explanation.surface: A man wildly sets fire to the oat crop, behaving like a beast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'madly' rearranges BURNS OUR OATS.
explanation.definitionFit: A huge long-necked dinosaur is a prehistoric creature of monstrous size.
